passage: I'm Jagdish, Kunal's hostel roommate. Last night a video went round every group we're in: a crowd, a burning shop, and a caption blaming "those people" from the next district. The music was dramatic, the voice angry. Half our floor shared it within minutes. Kunal watched it twice with his jaw set, and I thought he'd forward it too. Instead he paused on a signboard in the background, searched the shop's name, and found the same clip from three years ago, in another state, after a gas cylinder fire. Then he read two news reports about the district, from opposite sides, before posting in our group: "Old video, different place. Check before sharing." A few people left the group. I still don't know what he was thinking during that second viewing.

qa.q: What did the caption blame for the burning shop?
qa.a: It blamed "those people" from the next district.

qa.q: What does Kunal's set jaw during the second viewing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt angry or disturbed at first, pulled by the video's emotion, before he chose to check.

qa.q: Which of Kunal's steps is most useful for anyone who sees a viral clip?
qa.a: Pausing on a detail and searching for the original source showed the clip was old and from elsewhere, before any sharing.

qa.q: How does Jagdish see Kunal's response?
qa.a: Jagdish expected Kunal to forward it and is struck by the careful checking, though unsure what Kunal was thinking.

grounding: Shows a young adult resisting an emotionally charged viral clip, tracing its source and reading both sides, seen by a roommate.

passage:
Diary, Thursday
First real negotiation today. Jeevan, who runs the café near college, wanted me to design his new menu and posters for ₹2,000 and "exposure". My stomach was in knots all morning. I'd written down what the work actually takes: three drafts, print files, about twenty hours. I showed him the list instead of just saying "too low". He said money was tight since the rains flooded his storeroom. So we traded: ₹4,000, two drafts instead of three, and my name on the menu with a link to my page. He also threw in free coffee through exams, which, honestly, might be worth more. We shook on it, and I emailed a one-page summary so we both remember. I walked out feeling about two inches taller.
Ujjwal

qa.q: What did Jeevan first offer for the menu and posters?
qa.a: ₹2,000 and "exposure".

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel before the meeting?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt nervous, with a stomach in knots all morning.

qa.q: What made Ujjwal's negotiation fair to both sides?
qa.a: Showing the real work involved, hearing Jeevan's storeroom problem, and trading fewer drafts for a better fee found a middle both could accept, confirmed in writing.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see the final deal?
qa.a: Jeevan probably feels respected, since the tight budget was heard and he still gets his menu and posters.

grounding: Illustrates a young freelancer standing up for fair pay and reaching a written compromise with a small-business client.

passage: On move-in day at the college hostel in Warangal, Harish's father tightened the last screw on the rickety shelf and stood back. "That's it, then." Harish walked him to the gate, both of them too cheerful. When the auto pulled away, Harish felt his throat close up, and at the same time a strange lightness, like a window opening. Back in Room 214 his new roommate Sumit was sticking a map on the wall. "Canteen's open till eleven," Sumit said. "No one tells us when to sleep." Harish grinned. "No one." Then he sat on his bed, opened his bag, and found the steel tiffin his mother had packed, with a note: "Eat properly." He laughed and blinked hard at the same time.

qa.q: What was the number of Harish's hostel room?
qa.a: Room 214.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Harish have when the auto pulled away?
qa.a: He felt sad and a little scared, his throat closing up, but also excited and light at his new freedom.

qa.q: How could Harish make the first weeks easier on both feelings?
qa.a: He could call home regularly while also joining hostel life with Sumit, giving both the missing and the excitement some space.

qa.q: How does Sumit seem to experience move-in day?
qa.a: Sumit seems mostly excited, focused on the freedom of late canteen hours and no bedtime. 😄

grounding: Shows a young adult holding sadness and excitement at the same time on his first day away from home.

passage:
Dear Pradeep,
I walked past our old school today and saw they've cut down the gulmohar tree we used to climb after exams. I just stood there. Remember hiding the cricket ball in its roots so Kannan couldn't take it home? Back then the biggest worry was whether Ammi would notice my torn shorts. Now it's rent, internships and helping plan a cousin's wedding. Sometimes I'm a bit angry that nobody warned us how fast it goes. But I also remember you sharing your lunch every day in Class 4 when Abbu's shop was shut. That still feels like the safest I've ever been. Come home for Eid. We'll find another tree.
Imran

qa.q: What tree was cut down at the old school?
qa.a: The gulmohar tree they used to climb after exams.

qa.q: How did Imran feel standing by the spot where the tree had been?
qa.a: Imran felt a bittersweet longing for childhood, with a little anger that it all went so fast.

qa.q: What could Imran do with this nostalgic feeling?
qa.a: Reaching out to Pradeep, as the letter does, turns the longing into reconnection, like meeting at Eid to make new memories.

qa.q: What might it mean to Pradeep to read about the shared lunches?
qa.a: Pradeep would likely feel touched to learn that a small childhood kindness made Imran feel so safe. 🤍

grounding: Illustrates a young adult's bittersweet longing for the safety of childhood, written to an old friend.

passage: I'm Abhinav, Gopika's younger brother. The offer letter from the Bengaluru firm came on Monday, and since then my sister hasn't sat still. She's stuck three lists on the fridge: "Flat", "Things to learn", "Places to eat". Last night I found her on the terrace at midnight, looking up metro routes on her laptop and humming. At dinner she talked for twenty minutes about buying her own kettle, as if it were a sports car. Amma asked if she was nervous. "A bit," she said, and then immediately started planning which Saturday she'd join a cycling group. I don't know what she feels underneath, but I've never seen her eyes this bright.

qa.q: How many lists has Gopika stuck on the fridge?
qa.a: She has stuck three lists on the fridge.

qa.q: What does Gopika talking about her own kettle suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels eager and excited about even small parts of running her own life.

qa.q: How could Gopika use this energy well before she moves?
qa.a: She could turn the lists into a few concrete steps, like shortlisting flats and contacting the cycling group, while leaving room for surprises.

qa.q: How does Abhinav see his sister's excitement?
qa.a: Abhinav notices her bright eyes and constant planning, though he can't be sure what she feels underneath.

grounding: Shows a young adult's eager, forward-looking energy after a job offer in a new city, seen by her brother.

passage:
Diary, Sunday night
I've been staring at the same pile for two hours. Lease renewal due Friday. The HR form about my provident fund. A letter about Papa's health insurance that now needs my signature, since I'm the only one of us in Mohali. The gas cylinder booking. My first project deadline at work. Every time I pick one up, the others scream louder, and I put it down again. I actually lay on the floor for a while. Tejas came over with rajma-chawal and didn't lecture me. He just made me write each thing on a sticky note and put them in order of date. Five notes. Only one was due tomorrow: the gas booking. I did it in four minutes. The rest I'll ask HR and Papa's insurance agent about on Monday.
Gurleen

qa.q: How many sticky notes did Gurleen end up with?
qa.a: Five notes.

qa.q: How was Gurleen feeling while staring at the pile?
qa.a: Gurleen felt overwhelmed and stuck, so flooded by everything at once that nothing got done.

qa.q: Why did Tejas's sticky-note method help?
qa.a: Putting each task on its own note and ordering by date showed that only one was urgent, which broke the freeze and let Gurleen act.

qa.q: How does Tejas support Gurleen without taking over?
qa.a: Tejas brings food, doesn't lecture, and just helps sort the tasks, leaving Gurleen to do them.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult frozen by a sudden pile of permanent adult responsibilities and a friend's help in breaking it down.

passage: The apartment in Lisbon still had two coffee cups in the drying rack when Rania came back from the station. Tomás had taken the rest of his things that morning, after four years, and after all the evenings they'd spent planning the flat in Porto they would never rent. She sat on the kitchen floor with his cup in her hands and didn't cry for a long time. Then she did, for an hour. Her friend Ines arrived with soup and didn't ask questions. Later Rania said, "It isn't only him I'm missing. It's the whole life I'd already moved into in my head." Ines nodded and stayed the night on the sofa. In the morning Rania put one cup away.

qa.q: How long had Rania and Tomás been together?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: What does Rania mean by missing "the whole life I'd already moved into in my head"?
qa.a: She is grieving not just Tomás but the future they planned in Porto, a deep sorrow for an imagined life that is now gone.

qa.q: What helped Rania through the first night?
qa.a: Letting herself cry, and having Ines there with soup and no questions, gave her room to grieve without being alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Ines to stay the night?
qa.a: Ines probably feels sad for Rania and chooses quiet presence over advice, which seems to be what Rania needs.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving both a long relationship and the future she had imagined with him.

passage:
Journal, 3 March
The embassy email came this morning: visa refused, and the course starts in six weeks, so there's no time to reapply. For about an hour I drafted angry replies I'll never send. Then I called Suraj, who just listened and said, "That's really rough." Walking by the lake this evening, I noticed I'd stopped rehearsing arguments. The letter isn't going to change. What I still have: the admission can be deferred a year, my job at the lab is still open, and Ma was quietly relieved I'm not leaving yet. I'm not happy about it. But I'm not fighting it anymore either. Tomorrow I'll email the university about deferring, and ask Dr Rao if I can stay on the soil project.
Anirban

qa.q: How long until the course starts?
qa.a: The course starts in six weeks.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel walking by the lake that evening?
qa.a: Anirban still felt sad but calmer and more at peace, no longer rehearsing arguments against the refusal.

qa.q: What makes Anirban's plan for tomorrow a sign of acceptance?
qa.a: Instead of fighting the refusal, Anirban works with what remains, asking to defer the admission and stay on the soil project.

qa.q: How might Ma feel about the visa news?
qa.a: Ma seems quietly relieved to keep her child home a little longer, while knowing Anirban is disappointed.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult moving from anger to accepting a visa refusal and working with what remains.

passage:
Coach's note, district stadium, Saturday
Jeevan missed the fire-service physical last year by four seconds on the 1.6 km run. He didn't come to the ground for a month after. When he came back in January, he asked me to be honest about his form, and I was: his pacing fell apart after the second lap. He has been at the track at 5:30 every morning since, with his friend Tejas pacing him on a cycle. Two weeks ago he pulled a calf muscle and had to rest; I saw him sitting in the stands watching the others, jaw tight. He was back as soon as the physio cleared him. Today he ran it eleven seconds faster than last year. I've entered him for the next recruitment.

qa.q: By how many seconds did Jeevan miss the physical last year?
qa.a: By four seconds on the 1.6 km run.

qa.q: What does Jeevan's tight jaw in the stands suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt frustrated and restless at being sidelined, but determined not to give up.

qa.q: What helped Jeevan try again after the setback?
qa.a: Asking for honest feedback, training steadily with a pacing partner, and resting the injury properly until the physio cleared him.

qa.q: How does the coach see Jeevan's comeback?
qa.a: The coach respects his steady effort and shows faith in him by entering him for the next recruitment.

grounding: Shows a young adult rebuilding after failing a recruitment test and an injury, observed by his coach.

passage:
Diary, Saturday
This week I worked till ten every night on the audit and forgot what my face looks like when it isn't frowning. Today Anirban turned up at noon with a carrom board strapped to his scooter and refused to leave until I played. I said I had emails. He said, "The emails will still be boring at four." We played on the balcony for three hours. I lost six games, accused him of cheating with the powder, and laughed so hard at his victory dance that tea came out of my nose. My neck, stiff all week, stopped aching somewhere around game four. The emails were still boring at four. I finished them in forty minutes.
Vishal

qa.q: What did Anirban bring strapped to his scooter?
qa.a: A carrom board.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel during the carrom games?
qa.a: Vishal felt amused and relaxed, laughing so hard that tea came out, with the week's tension easing. 😄

qa.q: What does the afternoon suggest about balancing work and play?
qa.a: A few hours of play didn't hurt the work; the emails took only forty minutes, so making room for fun can help rather than hinder.

qa.q: Why might Anirban insist on staying until Vishal played?
qa.a: Anirban likely noticed how stressed Vishal had been and cared enough to push for a break.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult rediscovering play and laughter as a counterweight to work stress.
